narrative:
The model determined that you have a 69% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is substantially higher than what the admissions committee considers acceptable, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.60 was the strongest influence, pulling the prediction strongly toward failure. Compared with students who were accepted, whose average GPA is 3.23, your grades were noticeably lower and signaled to the model a higher likelihood of struggling with the bar exam.

Next in importance was your family income bracket. Being in the Middle-income group pushed the prediction further toward failure. While many accepted students also come from middle-income families, this characteristic still contributed negatively in your overall profile.

Your LSAT score of 34 was the third most influential factor. It is below the average of 37.18 among accepted students and therefore also nudged the outcome toward a higher risk of failing the bar.

Taken together, these elements created a profile the model viewed as carrying too great a chance of bar exam failure, leading to the rejection.

What you should do next is focus on improving the areas within your control. Retake the LSAT and aim for a meaningfully higher score, strengthen your study habits to raise your grades if you have additional coursework left, and consider bar exam preparation resources early. With targeted improvement, especially on the LSAT and academic performance, you can materially change your profile for future applications.
